title: Homophones
keyIdea: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings, such as brake and break, piece and peace, or meat and meet. You cannot hear which one is meant, so you choose the spelling from the meaning of the sentence. Clues hidden inside a spelling help: you hear with your ear, you eat meat, and a piece of pie. there is a place, their means it belongs to them, and they're is short for they are. The sound ay can also be spelt ei (vein), eigh (eight, weigh) or ey (they, grey).
familyTip: Play 'which one?' at dinner. Say a sentence such as 'Pass me a piece of bread' and ask your child to write or point to the right spelling: piece or peace. Then hunt for the hidden clue together: pie in piece, ear in hear, eat in meat. For there, their and they're, teach the swap test: if 'they are' fits the gap, write they're.

visual.caption: How is the ay sound spelt? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: a picture picks the spelling, sort there/their/they're, find clues inside words, build ay words with ei, eigh, ey, and fix mix-ups.

kid: Say brake and break out loud. They sound just the same. But a brake stops your bike, and to break means to smash. Words like this are called homophones. You can't hear which one to write, so think about what the sentence means.
Look for a clue inside the word. You hear with your ear. You eat meat. A piece of pie. Here, there and where are all place words.
Three words trip up lots of writers. there is a place. their means it belongs to them. they're means they are. If 'they are' fits, write they're.
The sound ay has some odd spellings too. It is ei in vein, eigh in eight and weigh, and ey in they and grey.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. The National Curriculum in England (English Appendix 1, Years 3 and 4) gives a list of homophones and near-homophones to learn. It includes brake/break, grate/great, here/hear, heel/heal, meat/meet, peace/piece, plain/plane, rain/rein/reign, scene/seen, weather/whether and whose/who's. The same list teaches the ay sound spelt ei (vein), eigh (eight, weigh, sleigh) and ey (they, obey, grey). there, their and they're come from Year 2 and are revisited here.

Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning, so phonics alone cannot pick between them. The habit to build is to read the whole sentence, decide what the word means, then choose the spelling. Clues inside the spelling help a lot: ear in hear, eat in meat, pie in piece, here in there and where. The 'they are' swap test sorts they're from there and their.

Common mistakes: choosing by sound alone (I can here you, press the break); always writing the more familiar word of a pair; swapping letters, as in peice; using their for 'there is'; and spelling the ay sound by ear, as in thay or ayt. Be careful with near-homophones such as accept and except, which sound alike but not the same.

In the lab your child picks the spelling that matches a picture sentence, sorts six there, their and they're gaps with the swap test, taps the clue letters hidden in five words, builds six ay words from ei, eigh or ey, and fixes four sentences with a wrong homophone. Each wrong move says why, for example 'peace means calm'.

practice.prompt: Which word fits? I ate a ___ of cake.
practice.hint: A part of something. Think: a piece of pie.
practice.explain: piece means a part of something. peace means calm, and peice is not a word.

practice.prompt: Sam finds {n} pairs of homophones, like meat and meet. How many words is that?
practice.hint: Each pair has two words that sound the same.
practice.explain: Two words in each pair, so {n} pairs make {=2*n} words.

practice.prompt: Which word fits? ___ dog is barking.
practice.hint: Ask who owns the dog. It belongs to them.
practice.explain: Their shows the dog belongs to them. There is a place, and They're means they are.

practice.prompt: A list has {n} words with the ay sound. {k} of them are spelt with eigh, like eight. The rest use ey, like they. How many use ey?
practice.hint: Take the eigh words away from the whole list.
practice.explain: {n} words take away {k} eigh words leaves {=n-k} ey words.

practice.hint: The ay sound in this word is spelt e, y.
practice.explain: they uses ey for the ay sound, like grey and obey.

choices: Words that sound the same but mean different things
Words that mean the same thing
Words that rhyme with each other
pool.explain: Homophones sound exactly the same but have different meanings and spellings, like brake and break.

pool.prompt: Which word fits? Squeeze the ___ to stop.
pool.hint: You want the part of a bike that stops it.
pool.explain: brake is the stopping part. break means to smash, or a rest.

pool.prompt: Which word fits? I think ___ lost.
pool.hint: Try the swap test: does 'they are' fit?
pool.explain: I think they are lost, so write they're.

pool.prompt: Which clue helps you spell hear?
pool.hint: Look for a small word hidden inside hear.
pool.explain: hear has ear inside it, and you hear with your ear.

pool.prompt: Ella writes {n} sentences. She fixes {k} wrong homophones. The rest were right. How many were right?
pool.hint: Take the fixed sentences away from all of them.
pool.explain: {n} sentences take away {k} fixed leaves {=n-k} that were right.

pool.prompt: Which is the number after seven?
pool.hint: It is spelt with eigh, like weigh.
pool.explain: The number is eight. ate is the past of eat, and ayt is not a word.

pool.hint: meat is food. Which word means come together?
pool.explain: meet means come together. You eat meat, so meat is the food.

pool.prompt: Which word means calm, with no fighting?
pool.hint: piece has pie in it, so it is the part one.
pool.explain: peace means calm. piece means a part, like a piece of pie.

pool.prompt: Which word fits? A ___ flew over the town.
pool.explain: plane is a flying machine. plain means simple, or flat land.

pool.prompt: A word bank has {n} homophone pairs, like plain and plane. Tom learns {k} pairs this week. How many pairs are left to learn?
pool.hint: Take the pairs Tom has learned away from all the pairs.
pool.explain: {n} pairs take away {k} learned leaves {=n-k} pairs to learn.
